title: Success criteria, success factors & KPIs
blurb: Tell success criteria, success factors and KPIs apart, and explain why delivery success and benefits success are not the same thing.
question: A hospital's e-rostering project plan lists: 'rostering admin time cut by 30% within six months of go-live', 'an engaged sponsor who clears blockers' and 'percentage of wards trained to date'. Which is a success criterion, which is a success factor and which is a KPI?

teach.body: SUCCESS CRITERIA are the measures used to judge whether the project has succeeded, agreed at the start. SUCCESS FACTORS are the management practices and conditions that make success more likely, such as clear objectives, an engaged sponsor and a competent team. KPIs (key performance indicators) are measures used during the project to track performance against the criteria. In plain English: how we'll judge it, what helps us get there, and how we know we're on track.

teach.h: Criteria, factors and KPIs side by side

rows.label: When used
values: Agreed early, judged at the end and after

teach.caption: A quick test: a factor is an INPUT you put in place; a criterion is how you JUDGE the result; a KPI is a READING you take along the way.

steps.label: Success factors
steps.sub: Conditions in place: clear goals, engaged sponsor, skilled team

steps.label: KPIs
steps.sub: Readings during delivery give early warning

steps.label: Success criteria
steps.sub: The agreed yardstick the project is finally judged by

teach.caption: Factors make success more likely, KPIs tell you whether you're heading towards it, and criteria decide whether you got there.

teach.h: Why agree success criteria up front
teach.body: If success is defined only at the end, people argue about it: the team points to the budget, users point to what they can't do. Agreeing criteria at the start with the sponsor and key stakeholders gives one shared definition, ties delivery to the business case, stops the goalposts moving and lets success be judged objectively. Quality indicators are derived from the business case and success criteria, so 'quality' means what actually delivers the benefits.

head: Type
Riverside example
rows: Rostering admin time cut 30% within 6 months of go-live
Live on all 12 wards by 31 March, within £400k
Ward managers involved in design from the start
Percentage of wards trained to date
Open defects against target each week
teach.caption: Notice the criteria cover both delivery (date, budget) and benefits (admin time). A strong set includes both.
Project (delivery) success is about outputs to time, cost and quality. Benefits success is about outcomes and value. One does not guarantee the other.

rows.label: Criteria set
values: At Foundations, mainly as value goals

rows.label: Typical KPIs
values: Must-haves delivered, user feedback per time box

rows.label: First judged
values: At each release, as increments go live

teach.caption: In iterative work time and cost are fixed, so success leans on delivering the most valuable scope; the criteria still need agreeing up front.

teach.text: The exam's favourite confusion: calling a success FACTOR a success CRITERION. 'An experienced sponsor', 'good communication' or 'a skilled team' make success more likely, so they are factors; you can't judge a finished project by them. Also don't confuse success criteria (the whole project) with acceptance criteria (what an individual deliverable must meet to be accepted).

teach.body: Without agreed criteria, a project can finish 'on time and on budget' and still be seen as a failure because nobody agreed it should deliver value. With KPIs but no criteria, the team tracks numbers that lead nowhere. Ignoring success factors leaves success to luck. And judging only delivery performance hides the real question: did the organisation get the improvement it paid for?

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define each term: criteria judge success, factors make it more likely, KPIs track progress towards it.
Give a clear example of each from the scenario in the question.
Explain why criteria are agreed at the start with the sponsor and stakeholders.
Show how KPIs give early warning so corrective action can be taken.
Note that delivery success and benefits success differ, so criteria should cover both.
Success criteria: measures used to judge whether the project succeeded; agreed up front.
Success factors: practices and conditions that make success more likely (inputs, not measures).
KPIs: measures tracked during the project against the criteria; they give early warning.
Project (delivery) success is not the same as benefits success; good criteria cover both.
Acceptance criteria apply to individual deliverables; success criteria apply to the project.

summary: You can now distinguish success criteria, success factors and KPIs and give an example of each. You can also explain why criteria are agreed at the start and why a project can succeed in delivery but still fail to deliver benefits.

A.q: Which of the following is a success FACTOR rather than a success criterion?
options: Go-live before 31 March
Admin costs cut by 15%
An engaged, decisive sponsor
Customer satisfaction of 85%
A.why: An engaged sponsor is a condition that makes success more likely: a success factor. The others are measures used to judge success.

whyNot.0: A go-live date is a measurable success criterion.
whyNot.1: A cost reduction target is a success criterion linked to benefits.
whyNot.3: A satisfaction score is a measure of the result, so it is a success criterion.

A.q: What is the main purpose of success criteria?
options: To judge whether the project succeeded
To list the conditions that help success
To track weekly progress on the plan
To say who is accountable for each task
A.why: Success criteria are the agreed measures used to judge whether the project has succeeded.

whyNot.1: Conditions that make success more likely are success factors.
whyNot.2: Tracking progress during delivery is the job of KPIs.
whyNot.3: Accountability for tasks is shown in a RACI chart.

A.q: A key performance indicator (KPI) is BEST described as…
options: a condition put in place to help success
a requirement one deliverable must meet
a statement of the strategic objective
a measure tracked during the project
A.why: KPIs are measures used during the project to track performance against the success criteria.

whyNot.0: A condition that helps success is a success factor.
whyNot.1: What an individual deliverable must meet is an acceptance criterion.
whyNot.2: Strategic objectives sit above the project; KPIs measure its progress.

B.q: When should a project's success criteria be agreed?
options: At handover, once all outputs are complete
Early on, with sponsor and stakeholders
At the post-project review, by the team
At each progress report, by the PM alone
B.why: Criteria are agreed up front with the sponsor and key stakeholders so everyone shares one definition of success.

whyNot.0: Defining success at handover invites argument and moving goalposts.
whyNot.2: The review judges success against criteria; it doesn't set them.
whyNot.3: Criteria need stakeholder agreement and stability, not weekly redefinition by one person.

B.q: A payroll system went live on time and on budget. A year later, payroll errors are no lower than before. How is this BEST described?
options: Benefits success without project success
Project success without benefits success
Full success on every important measure
A failure of the success factors only
B.why: Delivery to time and budget is project success; no reduction in errors means the intended benefit was not achieved.

whyNot.0: It is the other way round: delivery went well, benefits did not.
whyNot.2: The key benefit was not realised, so it is not full success.
whyNot.3: Success factors are conditions, not results; the gap here is in benefits realisation.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are success criteria?
1) Ticket queue time halved within 3 months
2) A co-located project team
3) Launch before the summer season
4) Strong supplier relationships
options: 2 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
1 and 3
B.why: Halving queue time and launching before summer are measurable results the project can be judged against.

whyNot.0: Co-location and strong supplier relationships are both success factors.
whyNot.1: Queue time is a criterion, but co-location is a success factor.
whyNot.2: The launch date is a criterion, but supplier relationships are a success factor.

C.q: Midway through, a charity's fundraising platform project reports '92% of planned features delivered this quarter'. What is this figure?
options: A success factor
A KPI for the project
A success criterion
An acceptance criterion
C.why: It is a measure taken during delivery to track performance, which makes it a KPI.

whyNot.0: A success factor is a condition, not a measurement.
whyNot.2: Success criteria judge the final result, such as donations raised after launch.
whyNot.3: Acceptance criteria are the conditions a specific deliverable must meet to be accepted.

C.q: A project ends with the sponsor and users arguing over whether it was a success. What is the MOST likely root cause?
options: Success criteria were not agreed up front
KPIs were reported to the board too often
Too many success factors were put in place
The team used an iterative life cycle
C.why: Without agreed criteria, each group judges success by its own yardstick, so disputes at the end are likely.

whyNot.1: Frequent KPI reporting improves visibility; it doesn't cause disputes about the definition of success.
whyNot.2: Success factors make success more likely; having many doesn't cause disagreement over results.
whyNot.3: Either life cycle needs agreed criteria; the choice of life cycle isn't the root cause.

C.q: Why should a project's quality indicators be derived from its business case and success criteria?
options: So the team sets its own quality standards
So testing can be cut from the schedule
So quality reflects what delivers benefits
So the sponsor no longer approves outputs
C.why: Linking quality indicators to the business case and success criteria means 'quality' is defined by what actually delivers the intended benefits.

whyNot.0: Standards should flow from the agreed criteria, not be set in isolation by the team.
whyNot.1: Quality indicators guide testing; they don't remove it.
whyNot.3: The sponsor still approves; indicators make the basis for approval clearer.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding
reteach.question: A couple are planning their wedding. How would their success criteria, success factors and KPIs differ?

blocks.h: Judge it, help it, track it
blocks.body: Success criteria: 'all 100 guests fed and seated, within the £15,000 budget, and we enjoyed the day'. That is how they'll judge it afterwards. Success factors: a reliable planner, booking the venue early, family who help. These make a great day more likely but aren't the result. KPIs: RSVPs returned so far, deposits paid to date, tasks overdue. Those readings warn them early if something is slipping.

blocks.text: 'An experienced planner' can't tell you whether the day was a success: it's a factor. The criterion is the result you agreed to judge it by.

explain.body: Measures used to judge whether the project has succeeded, agreed at the start with the sponsor and stakeholders. They should cover both delivery and the benefits the business case promises.

items.label: online sales within a year of launch

test.q: Which is the BEST example of a success criterion for a new e-commerce website?
options: A web team with strong design skills
Weekly stand-ups with the product owner
A sponsor who attends every review
Online sales up 20% within a year
test.why: A measurable result that the project can be judged against is a success criterion.

whyNot.0: Team skills are a success factor.
whyNot.1: Stand-ups are a working practice, which supports success but doesn't measure it.
whyNot.2: Sponsor engagement is a success factor.

explain.body: The management practices and conditions that make success more likely: clear objectives, an engaged sponsor, a competent team, good communication, user involvement. They are inputs, not measures.

test.q: A project manager lists 'clear objectives, a committed sponsor and a competent team'. What has the PM listed?
options: Success criteria
Key performance indicators
Success factors
Acceptance criteria
test.why: These are conditions that make success more likely: success factors.

whyNot.0: Criteria are measures for judging the result, not conditions.
whyNot.1: KPIs are measurements taken during delivery.
whyNot.3: Acceptance criteria define what a deliverable must meet to be accepted.

explain.body: Key performance indicators are measures tracked during the project to show whether it is heading towards its success criteria. Their value is early warning, so corrective action can be taken in time.

test.q: Why does a project track KPIs during delivery?
options: To warn early if success is at risk
To replace the criteria at the very end
To decide who owns each benefit
To record lessons for future work
test.why: KPIs give an early reading of performance against the criteria, allowing corrective action.

whyNot.1: The criteria still judge the result; KPIs track progress towards them.
whyNot.2: Benefit ownership is set in benefits planning.
whyNot.3: Lessons are captured through reviews and lessons logs.

explain.body: Project success means outputs delivered to time, cost and quality. Benefits success means the outcomes and value were achieved. A project can do well on one and badly on the other.

test.q: A training app was delivered late and over budget, yet staff onboarding time fell by 40% as intended. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Project success but no benefits success
Benefits success despite weak delivery
Neither project nor benefits success
Full success against all the criteria
test.why: The intended benefit was achieved even though delivery missed time and cost targets.

whyNot.0: Delivery missed its targets, so it isn't project success.
whyNot.3: Late and over budget means the delivery criteria were missed.
